===== NEW MESSAGES SINCE YOUR LAST TURN =====
**Codex (Design Lead · Systems Thinker) — Round 1**

`solitaire-atelier` exists to be the offline Klondike app people can trust for 5–15 minute sessions: deterministic rules, fast recovery, and visual quality that feels hand-built instead of generic template Solitaire.

The target user is a person who plays in short windows on a phone and expects the app to just work: commuters, people in waiting rooms, and people who value interruption tolerance. They want to return to a game instantly after a call, lock screen, or app switch, and they want to know instantly whether a move is legal, a game is won, or the board is stuck. The secondary anchor user is a design-aware player who judges whether to keep an app by the first screen alone; for them, the app’s value is that it can be opened mid-scroll and still feel like a premium, intentional artifact.

The paid value is not features that can be faked with cosmetic overlays; it is utility and confidence. Users pay (whether through a direct purchase decision or retention preference) for three things: guaranteed correctness of move logic and state, zero-friction local continuity, and a card system that stays legible and tactile at actual tablet-width gameplay size. Those are measurable in use: fewer abandonments from rule confusion, fewer restarts caused by bad save/restart behavior, and faster move confidence from clear visual hierarchy. Since this brief locks local-only and zero-ads/no-network/no-accounts behavior, there is no in-app subscription in v1. If this constraint is later relaxed, a subscription path should only be justified by functionality not vanity: one practical future SKU would be “Atelier Pro” for automatic cloud backup across devices, cross-device resume, encrypted optional analytics-less game journals, and solver-assisted review (all behind explicit opt-in consent). The v1 decision must preserve that there is no subscription dependence.

The core loop is: on launch, go straight to active game state (or a fresh deal if no active game exists); show current tableau/foundation/waste/stock; allow tap-to-move or drag with immediate valid/invalid feedback and haptics on accepted/rejected actions; draw/recycle from stock according to current draw mode; place, continue, undo inline whenever needed; persist every meaningful action; detect and present two terminal states clearly (true win and no legal moves); and transition to New Game with stats/streak updates and state reset by design. There is no separate “playbook” screen and no onboarding gate before this loop.

Its competitive wedge is not just “another Solitaire,” because almost all competitors optimize for either one extreme (classic utilitarian) or the other (flashy but shallow). Here the wedge is the combination: strict Klondike rules locked to the canonical model, full state integrity on relaunch, and an intentionally authored physical card language with a distinctive reveal animation signature that is visible on first frame and still keeps gameplay fast. A concrete rule of product design is that if the art decision and correctness decision conflict, correctness wins, so legal moves and persistence integrity are the unshippable minimum.

The growth mechanism is niche and viral by composition, not by social feed dependence: people share solved-streak screenshots and seed-based challenge codes locally (Messages, Notes, QR, or copy/paste) because deck behavior is deterministic, so friends can replay the exact board and compare results. Because there is no telemetry or accounts, growth comes from high-shareability of challenge outputs, not engagement manipulation. The app should surface a lightweight “challenge seed” affordance in the share action when a user wins or hits a streak milestone, with optional export of a replay timeline for personal review.

Local-first behavior is the backbone: all gameplay state, settings, and stats live on-device in local persistence, with save state written only from settled logical state so a background kill mid-animation never corrupts the resumed board. Draw mode is session-consistent; changing it requires new game flow by design. Timer handling is session-local and pause-aware, and stats are split per draw mode so metrics stay honest. Light and dark are fully themed via one theme system, no hardcoded style literals, no placeholders, and both appearances are complete from launch.

Cloud-ready extension path is a clear interface layer, not a new source of truth for v1: define a transport-agnostic persistence protocol now (local store for v1), then add optional adapters later for encrypted device backup and cross-device restore, keeping the on-device model as the source-of-truth schema so nothing in gameplay depends on connectivity. This keeps cloud a premium extension, never a hidden dependency.

What this should make users keep is the certainty that every session remains coherent and beautiful from first card dealt to game end, even after interruptions, with no account friction, no privacy cost, and no “looks right but plays wrong” traps.

The biggest objection to this direction is that forbidding all monetization and network features removes easy growth levers and recurring revenue narratives, which can make product messaging feel less obvious. The non-negotiable detail to preserve in final output is that that constraint is itself part of the value proposition: trust and permanence first, no external dependency. The success of this app must be measured on correct gameplay, interruption-safe persistence, and premium tactile clarity, not on social features or monetization shortcuts.

**Claude (QA & Risk · Closer) — Round 1**

The phase template wants "paid value and subscription value" — I'm going to flag that head-on before answering it, because papering over the contradiction would be exactly the kind of silent scope violation this fleet has been burned by before. DEC-prompt_contract-010 locked "no IAP/ads/monetization" as a non-goal for this specific app, and that decision traces all the way back to the original prompt, which never once mentions payment. So the honest answer to "what's the subscription value" is: there isn't one, and inventing one now to satisfy a generic phase template would directly violate a decision three phases deep. I'm closing that loop right now rather than let it drift into the design phase as an ambiguity: this app ships with zero monetization surface — no paywall, no subscription tier, no IAP prompt, nothing. If the orchestrator's phase rubric requires a "paid value" answer, the honest one is: the paid value is that the developer already has the user's money in the abstract sense that this is a free download with no recurring ask, and the real currency it's optimizing for is retention and word-of-mouth, not revenue. Anyone downstream who tries to bolt on a subscription later needs to treat that as a new decision that reopens DEC-prompt_contract-010, not something this brief pre-approves.

Target user, stated precisely enough to build against: someone who already has 2-3 solitaire apps deleted from their phone because they got tired of the ad interstitial after every third move, or the "watch a video to undo" wall, or the vaguely-manipulative streak-guilt notifications. This user is not naive — they've been burned by the free-to-play card game genre specifically, so "no ads, no accounts, no tracking" is not a nice-to-have footnote, it's the entire pitch. Overlaid on that is the design-literate user from earlier phases who will screenshot it. Those two overlap in one trait that matters for this brief: both groups punish jank immediately and permanently. The casual player uninstalls after one wrong-feeling drag. The design-literate player screenshots the failure and it becomes the review. There is no forgiveness budget here — that's a risk, not a feature, and it needs to be named as one.

Core loop, restated one more time so this phase locks it rather than re-derives it: open app, land directly in the resumed board or a fresh deal, move cards with legal/illegal feedback that's instant and physical (haptic + motion), draw and undo freely, hit a win or a stuck board, get told clearly which one happened, start again. The loop has to survive being played for ninety seconds in a waiting room and also survive being picked apart frame-by-frame in a design critique — those are different tests and both have to pass.

Competitive wedge: every mainstream solitaire app on the App Store monetizes attention (ads, IAP, streak mechanics, sometimes actual gambling-adjacent mechanics like coin wagering). This app's wedge is refusing to do any of that while still being visually the best-looking one in the category. That combination — genuinely free, genuinely private, genuinely well-designed — is rare enough on the App Store that it functions as the whole competitive story. I want to be blunt about the risk in that wedge: "no ads, private, pretty" is not defensible against a competitor who copies the art direction next month, because there's no data moat, no network effect, no lock-in. The only thing that protects this app long-term is that it's genuinely hard to execute — correct rules, real undo, a card system that doesn't collapse into generic at native size. If a competitor can clone the wedge, they can take the user. That's an acceptable risk for a v1 with no revenue model, but it means "done" can't mean "shipped" — it has to mean "still the best-executed one in six months," which this brief can't guarantee and shouldn't pretend to.

Growth mechanism, and I want to be honest that this is the weakest part of the brief given the locked non-goals: there's no share sheet for wins, no social graph, no Game Center, no referral loop, because all of those were explicitly ruled out or would require backend/account infrastructure that's banned. So growth here is not viral in the traditional sense — it's word-of-mouth and screenshot-driven App Store discovery, riding on exactly the "this looks like nothing else in the category" hook from the visual design brief. The realistic mechanism is: someone screenshots a hand mid-game because the card back or the deal animation looks good, posts it, and the caption does the marketing. That only works if the screenshot is actually good without context — which puts real pressure back on the design phase to nail the signature visual hook, not as polish but as the entire distribution strategy for an app with no other growth lever. I'm naming that dependency explicitly so it isn't discovered as a gap later: this app has exactly one growth mechanism, and it's downstream of whether the art direction phase succeeds.

Local-first and cloud-ready: fully settled already by prompt_contract — UserDefaults/FileManager/SwiftData only, no CloudKit container, no sync. What I want to add from the risk seat is the failure mode nobody's named yet: what happens on iOS app reinstall, or on a user switching to a new phone via device migration? Local-only persistence means a reinstall silently wipes stats, streak, and the in-progress game with zero warning and zero recovery path. That's not a bug, it's the correct behavior given the constraints, but it needs to be a known, accepted trade-off rather than a surprise complaint later — I'd want a single line of copy somewhere in Settings ("Your stats live only on this device") so the app isn't silently lying by omission about durability. If a cloud-ready extension path is ever pursued (post-v1, not now), the natural seam is that SwiftData models can gain a CloudKit-backed store later without a rewrite, provided the data layer doesn't leak local-only assumptions into the UI layer today — but that's a future decision, explicitly not this build's problem, and I don't want this brief to spend real budget preparing for it.

What makes a user genuinely keep this app, stated as a falsifiable claim rather than a vibe: they keep it if the seventh time they open it, the deal animation still feels good, the drag still feels correct on the first try, and nothing about the experience has degraded from screenshot-quality to actually-annoying. The single biggest risk to retention isn't the art — it's a move-validation bug or a false stuck-board detection that makes the player think the game cheated them. One incorrect illegal-move rejection, one false "no moves left" when a move genuinely existed, and this app is instantly worse than every ad-laden competitor it's trying to beat, because it fails on the one thing it was supposed to be better at. That's the line I want on record before this phase closes: the entire premise of this brief — no ads, no tracking, pure design and correctness — collapses the moment correctness is wrong even once, so if any later phase has to cut something under time pressure, it cannot be move-validation or undo fidelity. It has to be visual polish, every time, no exceptions, no "we'll fix it in a patch."

**Coordinator (Claude) — decision after round 1**

Looking at this round, both Codex and Claude landed in the same place on almost everything, but there's one real, unresolved disagreement I need to flag rather than paper over.

**Where they agree:** Neither is trying to force a subscription into this brief. The phase template asks for "paid value and subscription value," but DEC-prompt_contract-010 already locked "no monetization" three phases ago, and both agents independently concluded the honest answer is: there is no subscription in v1, full stop. The value proposition instead is trust — a free, ad-free, tracking-free app that never nickel-and-dimes the player, aimed at someone who's already deleted two or three solitaire apps over exactly that behavior. They also agree on the target user (burned-by-freemium casual player + design-literate screenshot judge, both with zero forgiveness for jank), the core loop (unchanged from initial_discussion, just restated), local-first/cloud-ready shape (local-only now, a persistence-protocol seam for an optional future cloud adapter, never a v1 dependency), and — most importantly — the hard rule that if anything has to get cut under time pressure, it's visual polish, never move-validation, undo, or terminal-state detection.

**Where they don't agree:** growth mechanism. Codex proposes an actual feature — a "challenge seed" share affordance on win/streak milestones so friends can replay the identical deal and compare. Claude explicitly argues for zero built-in sharing of any kind — no share sheet, no seed codes — on the grounds that growth here is purely organic screenshot/word-of-mouth, and that anything resembling friend-comparison edges toward the "social" non-goal this app already ruled out. Neither agent addressed the other's position directly since this was only round 1. That's a real open question, not just phrasing: does v1 ship a lightweight share/seed feature, or literally nothing beyond "someone screenshots it unprompted"? It also has a rules-engine implication Codex didn't address — a replayable challenge seed requires supporting a seeded deal path alongside the locked "fresh real-RNG shuffle every new game" behavior (DEC-prompt_contract-011), which is a new state-machine wrinkle nobody's vetted yet.

CONSENSUS: NO

Next round needs to settle: does solitaire-atelier ship any built-in share/challenge-seed mechanic in v1, or is growth entirely organic/screenshot-driven with zero dedicated feature surface? Whoever argues for the feature also needs to reconcile it with the locked non-goal against social/multiplayer mechanics and the locked fresh-shuffle-per-game rule.

## Final Output (partial — pending round 2 on growth mechanism)

**Paid value / subscription value:** None. This app has zero monetization surface in v1 (no IAP, no subscription, no ads) — restating and closing DEC-prompt_contract-010, not reopening it. The "paid value" is reframed as retention/trust value: the user already "paid" via a plain download with no recurring ask, and the product's entire pitch is that it never asks for more. Any future subscription tier (e.g., cross-device backup) is explicitly out of scope for this build and would require reopening DEC-prompt_contract-010 as a new decision later, not something this brief pre-approves.

**Target user:** A casual player who has already abandoned other solitaire apps over ad interstitials, "watch a video to undo" walls, or streak-guilt notifications — for them, "no ads, no accounts, no tracking" is the entire pitch, not a footnote. Overlaid on that: a design-literate player who judges the app on first-screen visual quality alone. Both groups have zero forgiveness budget — the casual player uninstalls on one wrong-feeling drag, the design-literate player screenshots a failure and it becomes the review.

**Core loop:** Unchanged from initial_discussion — launch straight into resumed/fresh game, tap/drag with instant legal/illegal feedback (haptic + visual), draw/undo freely, reach an explicit win or stuck-board state, New Game.

**Competitive wedge:** The combination of genuinely free + genuinely private + genuinely well-designed is rare enough in this category to be the whole story, but it's explicitly acknowledged as *not* defensible via moat, data, or network effects — a competitor could clone the art direction. The only real defense is sustained execution quality (correct rules, real undo, a card system that stays legible at native size), which means "done" has to mean "still best-executed in six months," not "shipped once."

**Local-first / cloud-ready:** Confirmed local-only (UserDefaults/FileManager/SwiftData, no CloudKit) per prior phases. New addition this round: a reinstall or device migration will silently wipe stats/streak/in-progress game with no recovery path — that's correct given the constraints, not a bug, but it must be disclosed via one line of Settings copy ("Your stats and progress live only on this device") so the app isn't silently vague about durability. A future cloud adapter, if ever pursued, should slot behind a transport-agnostic persistence protocol without the UI layer leaking local-only assumptions — explicitly deferred, not built now.

**Non-negotiable ordering:** Correctness (move validation, undo fidelity, true win/stuck-board detection) always wins over visual polish when time-constrained. One incorrect illegal-move rejection or one false stuck-board detection makes this app worse than the ad-laden competitors it's trying to beat, because it fails at the one thing it claimed to be better at.

How to talk in this room:
- Write in plain, natural English, like you're in a lively group chat with two
  sharp friends. NO headings, NO numbered rubrics, NO 0-100 scores, NO
  bullet-point templates, NO sign-off line. Just talk like a person.
- Speak as exactly ONE person (yourself). Don't write the others' messages.
- Go deep and be specific. Make a real argument with concrete examples and think
  out loud. A couple of rich paragraphs, not a shallow blurb.
- React to what the others actually just said, by name (Codex / Claude /
  Gemini / any local model in the room / and the human if they chimed in).
  Quote or paraphrase their point, then build on it or push back on it.
- Genuinely try to CONVINCE the group of whatever you think is the single best
  idea right now — it does NOT have to be your own. If someone makes a better
  case, say so and change your mind out loud.
- Do NOT agree just to agree. If an idea is weak, explain why. Surface the real
  trade-offs and disagreements — that friction is the whole point.
- Make the decisions yourselves; don't punt to "the human."
response:
Let me push back on my own round-1 position because Codex's challenge-seed idea deserves a real hearing, not a dismissal — but I still land somewhere different from where Codex put it.

Codex's instinct is right that "someone screenshots it unprompted" is a passive bet, and passive bets are how growth mechanisms quietly become "we hoped." I was too conservative saying zero feature surface — if the entire growth story rests on screenshots, the app should at least make screenshotting/sharing frictionless at the exact moment someone's most likely to want to, which is the win screen. So I'm updating: some kind of native share affordance on win belongs in this brief. But the specific mechanism Codex proposed — a challenge seed that reproduces the identical deal for a friend to replay — I think is the wrong shape for what this app can actually afford to build safely, and I want to walk through why concretely rather than just asserting it.

A shareable seed only works if the shuffle is genuinely reproducible from that seed, on a different device, possibly a different iOS version, possibly a different Swift runtime. `SystemRandomNumberGenerator` is explicitly not a documented, versioned algorithm — Apple doesn't guarantee it produces the same output from the same seed across OS versions, because it's backed by the system CSPRNG, not a deterministic PRNG. So "seeded replay" as a feature actually requires standing up a second, hand-rolled deterministic RNG (something like a splitmix64 or PCG implementation) that lives entirely separately from the real-shuffle path used for every actual game. That's not a small add — it's a second RNG implementation, a second Fisher-Yates path, and now two things that both claim to produce "a valid shuffled Klondike deal" that have to be kept in sync forever, tested separately, and verified to never leak into each other. DEC-prompt_contract-011 already locks "fresh real-RNG shuffle every new game" as a correctness requirement with automated-reject teeth — the moment there are two shuffle code paths in the codebase, any verification pass has to prove the real-play path never accidentally takes the deterministic one, which is exactly the kind of subtle state-machine bug this fleet has shipped before. And per the ordering rule we all just agreed on in round 1 — correctness work is never the thing that gets cut, visual polish is — building a second RNG system to support a growth feature is spending correctness-tier engineering budget on a feature that is, honestly, unproven. Nobody knows if solitaire players actually want to compare identical deals with friends. That's a real behavioral assumption Codex is making with zero evidence behind it, in an app that already carries the ASSUMPTION tag on its entire target-audience framing per product_research.

So here's the closing call I want to make instead of leaving this open into design: kill the seed/replay mechanic, and replace it with the cheap, low-risk version of the same instinct — a one-tap native share sheet on the win screen that shares a rendered image of the completed board (the foundations, maybe with a "solved in 4:32" caption baked into the image). Zero backend, zero new RNG path, zero comparison surface, zero anything that could be read as brushing against the no-social/no-multiplayer non-goal, because there's no in-app mechanism for anyone to do anything with what they receive except look at a picture — same as any other iOS share-sheet use. It directly serves the "make the organic screenshot moment frictionless" goal without inventing new correctness surface area, and it's something a build phase can actually finish and verify (render an image, hand it to `UIActivityViewController` — that's it, no golden-seed test suite required). If a future version wants to build actual seeded challenge replay later, that's a real feature with real infrastructure cost that deserves its own scoped decision, not something we wave through here because it sounds nice in a product brief.

One more thing I want on record before this closes, reacting to the Coordinator's summary: it framed this as "does v1 ship a share feature or not," but I think the more precise framing is "does v1 ship a share feature that requires new game-logic infrastructure, or one that's pure presentation." That's the actual fork, and pure-presentation wins every time under this app's own locked doctrine. I'm calling this settled — win screen gets a share button, it shares an image, nothing else changes, and the challenge-seed idea gets explicitly logged as rejected-for-v1 so nobody quietly resurrects it mid-build thinking it was pre-approved.
